title: Palindrome Index
directAnswer: Walk two pointers from the ends inward. As long as s[left] == s[right], move in. At the first mismatch, exactly one of the two characters must go: test whether the inner substring s[left+1..right] is a palindrome — if so, remove left; otherwise remove right. If the pointers cross with no mismatch, the string is already a palindrome → return −1. O(n) time, O(1) space.

remember.formula:
l, r = 0, n-1
while l < r:
    if s[l] != s[r]:
        if isPalindrome(s, l+1, r): return l
        else: return r
    l++, r--
return -1
rules: At the first mismatch the removable index is **left** or **right** — decide by retesting the narrowed range.
Test `s[l+1..r]` (skip left): if it's a palindrome, removing **left** works → return `l`.
Otherwise removing **right** must work (the problem guarantees a solution) → return `r`.
No mismatch through the whole scan → already a palindrome → return **−1**.
The guarantee 'removing at most one char makes it a palindrome' means you never need to test both deeply.
whenToUse: Symmetric (palindrome) property checked from both ends
You may remove exactly one element and must locate which
A single localized mismatch decides the answer
O(1) extra space is desired — pointers, no copies
antiSignals: More than one deletion allowed → becomes a DP (longest palindromic subsequence)
Need the resulting string, not the index → build it after deciding
Insertions allowed instead of deletions → min-insertions DP
Case/space normalization required → preprocess first (Valid Palindrome II family)
remember.takeaway: Palindrome checks are two pointers converging from the ends. The first asymmetry pins down a single suspect on each side; retesting the range with one side skipped tells you which removal restores symmetry. The guarantee of a one-deletion fix lets you commit after a single retest.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you reach for converging two pointers on a palindrome and handle the 'which side to remove' decision with a single targeted re-check rather than brute-forcing every deletion.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Returning the first mismatch index without verifying which side actually fixes the palindrome, or forgetting the −1 case when the string is already a palindrome.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Explain that at the first mismatch only two candidates exist (left or right), and one O(n) sub-check decides between them — so the whole thing stays O(n), not O(n²).

problemStatement:
Given a string `s`, determine the **index** of a character that can be removed to make `s` a palindrome. There is **always a valid solution**: either the string is already a palindrome, or removing exactly one character makes it one.

If `s` is already a palindrome, return `-1`. Otherwise return the 0-based index of the character to remove. If multiple indices work, any valid one is acceptable.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters
A valid answer always exists (remove at most one character)
Return any valid index, or −1 if already a palindrome
understanding: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, so checking it is naturally a two-pointer walk from both ends. While the ends agree, the outer layer is symmetric and we peel inward. The moment they disagree, the culprit is one of those two mismatched characters. Because we're promised a one-deletion fix, removing the right suspect must turn the remaining string into a palindrome — we just have to figure out which suspect.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if it's already a palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Return −1 — no removal is needed. The two-pointer loop completes without a mismatch.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is a solution guaranteed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. The problem promises that removing at most one character yields a palindrome, so after the first mismatch one of the two sides is guaranteed to work.

clarifyingQuestions.question: If two indices both work, which do I return?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Any valid index. For 'aba' style ties, returning either symmetric position is accepted.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need to build the resulting palindrome?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No — only the index. The internal palindrome re-check uses index bounds, not new strings, to stay O(1) space.

examples.explanation: l=0 'a' vs r=3 'b' mismatch. Is s[1..3]="aab" a palindrome? No. So remove right index 3 → "aaa" is a palindrome.
l=0 'b' vs r=2 'a' mismatch. Is s[1..2]="aa" a palindrome? Yes. So remove left index 0 → "aa" is a palindrome.
Already a palindrome; pointers cross with no mismatch → −1.

approaches.name: Try Removing Each Index (Brute Force)
approaches.whenToMention: State it to anchor correctness, then note it's O(n²) and that two pointers find the suspect directly.
hints: The answer is some index i to delete. What's the most direct way to test a candidate?
For each i, form s with index i removed and check whether it's a palindrome.
Return the first i that works, or −1 if s is already a palindrome. Note this is n palindrome checks → O(n²).
approaches.complexityReasoning: Up to n candidate indices, each requiring an O(n) palindrome check on a length-(n−1) string → O(n²) time; building each candidate string costs O(n) space.
approaches.explanation:
Literally enumerate the answer: for each index `i`, delete it and test the result for palindromicity. Return the first index that produces a palindrome; if none is needed, return −1.

**Why it's correct.** The answer is by definition 'some index whose removal yields a palindrome'. Trying them all cannot miss it, and the first hit is a valid answer (the problem accepts any).

**Why we improve it.** Two pointers reveal the *only* indices worth trying. Everywhere the ends already match, deleting an interior matched character can't fix anything (the mismatch is elsewhere). So the entire search collapses to the first mismatch position and its mirror — two candidates, one re-check — instead of `n` full checks.
approaches.insight: Brute force tests every index; the two-pointer scan proves only two indices can possibly be the answer. Recognising that the first asymmetry localizes the suspects is what removes the outer O(n) factor.

dryRun.intro: Remove each index, test the leftover for palindromicity, return the first that works.

approaches.name: Two Pointers with One-Side Re-check (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The intended answer — converge from the ends, and at the first mismatch run a single inner palindrome test to pick the side.
hints: Checking a palindrome is a converging two-pointer walk. Where does that walk first break?
At the first l/r mismatch, the removable character is either s[l] or s[r] — nothing else.
Test whether skipping left (s[l+1..r]) is a palindrome: if yes return l, else return r. If the walk never breaks, return −1.
approaches.complexityReasoning: The outer walk is one pass, O(n). At most one inner palindrome check over a sub-range, also O(n). Total O(n) time, O(1) space (index arithmetic only — no string copies).
approaches.explanation:
Set `l = 0`, `r = n − 1`. While `s[l] == s[r]`, advance `l++`, `r--`. If the loop finishes, `s` is already a palindrome → return −1.

At the first mismatch, the two suspects are `s[l]` and `s[r]`. Run one targeted check: is `s[l+1 .. r]` a palindrome (i.e. would removing the left character fix it)? If yes, return `l`. Otherwise the only remaining possibility — guaranteed by the problem — is that removing the right character works, so return `r`.

**Why only two candidates exist.** Every step before the mismatch confirmed `s[l] == s[r]`, a symmetric matched layer. Deleting a character inside a matched layer can't repair a break that lives deeper in; it would only desynchronise the symmetry. So the break must be healed at the boundary where it appears — by dropping `s[l]` or `s[r]`.

**Why one re-check suffices.** The guarantee says some single deletion works. We test the 'skip left' range directly; if it's a palindrome we're done. If it isn't, we don't need to also verify 'skip right' — the guarantee forces it to be the answer. (You may verify it for safety, but it's logically implied.)

**Why O(1) space.** The inner check uses indices `l+1` and `r`, walking inward with two more pointers — no substring is materialized.

**Why this is O(n) not O(n²).** Unlike brute force, there is at most a single inner check, and it runs once at the unique first mismatch — not once per index.
approaches.insight: A palindrome's first point of asymmetry is a chokepoint: it localizes all possible answers to two positions. This 'find the break, then branch on a local repair' shape recurs in Valid Palindrome II and many greedy-on-symmetry problems.

First asymmetry: the answer is index l or r.

python.line: def is_pal(l: int, r: int) -> bool:
python.explanation: Index-bounded check — no substring copy, O(1) space.

python.line: return l if is_pal(l + 1, r) else r
python.explanation: One re-check decides which side to drop.

pitfalls: Returning the mismatch index without the inner re-check to pick the correct side.
Materializing substrings for the inner check instead of using index bounds (O(n) space).
Missing the −1 path when the string is already a palindrome.

commonMistakes: Returning the first mismatch index blindly without testing which side to remove.
Forgetting the −1 case for an already-palindromic string.
Using an O(n²) per-index deletion approach on large inputs.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Guessing the side at the mismatch
commonMistakesDetailed.why: At the first mismatch either s[l] or s[r] could be the culprit. Returning l (or r) without a re-check is wrong half the time — e.g. 'aaab' needs r, 'baa' needs l.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if s[l] != s[r]:
    return l   # blind guess
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if s[l] != s[r]:
    return l if is_pal(l + 1, r) else r

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Forgetting the already-palindrome case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If the loop never hits a mismatch the string is a palindrome and the answer is −1; falling through to return 0 (or l) is incorrect.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
while (l < r) { if (s.charAt(l) != s.charAt(r)) { ... } l++; r--; }
return 0;
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
while (l < r) { if (s.charAt(l) != s.charAt(r)) { ... } l++; r--; }
return -1;

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Copying substrings for the inner check
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Building s[l+1..r] as a new string costs O(n) memory and time on every call; pass index bounds instead to keep O(1) space.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
sub = s[l + 1:r + 1]
if sub == sub[::-1]: return l

patternNote: Two-pointer palindrome with localized repair. Converge from the ends; the first asymmetry pins the answer to two candidates, and a single inner re-check (skip one side) chooses between them. The 'find the break, branch locally' shape generalizes to Valid Palindrome II and one-edit problems.
